Area.evidence_source: In reviewing recent changes in their lives, these participants were able to articulate a sense of purpose and a vision of their future where they would be able to provide care for others, for example, infirmed or young family members, or the anticipation of a more financially stable life that would support their children in their home countries. While these changes in circumstances might not be deemed as significant improvement in the participants' quality of life, they certainly seemed to have fueled a sense of empowerment among the participants as they realized they could assume the role of reciprocating care in the family, a universal human need that was also amplified by the emphasis of interdependence in the Asian collectivistic cultures. A female participant who used to think that she should die when her parents pass away talked about why she had a change of heart: 'I don't have a lot of expectations for my life right now, but I realize that my younger brother may be dying (of cancer), and I need to take care of him and my parents.' A female participant talked with a sense of pride about how she took care of her family since her condition stabilized: 'My husband knows how to cook, but he wants me to do all the cooking. I also tidy the place every day so we can spend some family time together after dinner.'
